title: Area VI review: Airport and Seaplane Base Operations
intro: These questions mix the two ASEL Tasks of Area VI: communications, light signals and runway lighting, and traffic patterns. Most join them in one real instructing situation, such as a radio failure in a tower pattern or a quiet CTAF arrival, the way an examiner would ask.

questions.q: On a dual flight at a Class D airport both radios fail. Your learner stays outside the surface area until she knows the traffic flow, joins left downwind and sees a flashing green from the tower. She reaches for the flaps and says, "Green, so we're cleared to land." What do you teach?
options: Any green from the tower in flight is a landing clearance, steady or flashing, so she can finish the pattern and land without waiting for anything more
Flashing green in flight means the airport is unsafe and she must not land, so she should leave the pattern and fly to a nontowered field nearby
Flashing green in flight means return for landing, with steady green to follow, so she keeps flying the pattern and watching for the steady green
Flashing green is a ground signal that clears taxiing, so in flight it does not apply to her and she can land once she sees the runway is clear
questions.why: In flight, a flashing green means return for landing (to be followed by steady green at the proper time); only a steady green means cleared to land [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. With both radios dead the AIM has her join the pattern and keep visual contact with the tower for light signals [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]], and since a light can only approve or disapprove what she seems about to do, she must keep looking for the next one [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13]]. "Airport unsafe, do not land" is flashing red, not flashing green. Flashing green does clear an aircraft on the ground to taxi, but it also has an in-flight meaning [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. Teach her to ask "ground or air?" first, then "steady or flashing?"

questions.q: Arriving at a busy nontowered airport from the upwind side, your learner announces on the CTAF and crosses midfield 500 feet above the 1,000-foot AGL pattern altitude. No large or turbine aircraft use the field. Over the far side of the runway she pulls the power to descend in a turn straight onto downwind. What do you teach?
options: Her plan is fine: she crossed above the pattern, and the regulations govern only the direction of turns, so how she gets down to downwind is her own choice
She should have crossed midfield at pattern altitude instead; on a busy day the midfield crosswind entry is the preferred method because it is the quickest way in
Continue about 2 miles clear, scan, descend to pattern altitude there, then turn back to join on the 45 at midfield; patterns are entered level at TPA
She should leave the pattern area and come back for a straight-in, since a straight-in arrival keeps her well away from the airplanes on downwind
questions.why: The AFH's preferred upwind-side entry is to announce, cross midfield at least 500 feet above pattern altitude, and when well clear, about 2 miles, scan, descend to pattern altitude, then turn to enter on the 45 to downwind at midfield [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. Nontowered patterns are always entered at pattern altitude [[24:168|AFH 8-4]], and entries while descending create specific collision hazards [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]. True, the FAA regulates flow, not entry [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1]], but that makes the recommended entry the safe choice, not an optional one. The midfield crosswind entry at TPA is only the alternate and should not be used when the pattern is busy [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. A straight-in is not recommended with others in the pattern [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1]].

questions.q: Your learner is inbound VFR on flight following to a nontowered field with AWOS, 15 miles out. Approach reads her the wind at a towered airport 30 miles away. The field's AWOS gives a different wind and a lower ceiling. She plans to go by approach's numbers because 'ATC knows more.' What do you teach?
options: Neither matters at a nontowered field; she should land on whatever runway UNICOM gives her, since UNICOM has the most accurate local wind
Approach's report is official and overrides the AWOS, so she should ignore the field broadcast until she is close enough to see the wind sock
AWOS broadcasts are meant for IFR pilots, so she should use the towered airport's ATIS and then overfly the field at pattern altitude to read the wind sock
The field's one-minute AWOS is more current than what the controller has; use it, check the sock too, and tell approach she has the one-minute weather
questions.why: At an uncontrolled airport with ASOS/AWOS, the one-minute weather is available within about 25 NM below 10,000 feet, pilots have more current weather than controllers located miles away, controllers rely on the pilot to determine the current airport weather, and the pilot should tell the controller she has the one-minute weather when asking for service [[33:274|AIM 4-3-27]]. Check the wind indicators as well, because there is no assurance that radio information is accurate [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]]. AWOS is for every pilot, and the indicators are read from above pattern altitude before going well clear to descend, not by overflying at pattern altitude [[17:14|AC 90-66C 11.2]]. UNICOM is not required to answer and has no standards for what it says [[17:5|AC 90-66C 9.3]].

questions.q: At a towered airport your learner is number two on downwind, told to follow a Cherokee, and is closing on it fast. Without a word she rolls into a 360 for spacing. In the debrief, what do you teach?
options: Fit in early with speed or course changes; tell the controller before maneuvering for spacing, and never 360 in the pattern without advising first
She should have closed on the Cherokee and passed it on the left, since the overtaking airplane has the right-of-way once it is faster
She should have extended downwind silently instead, since once the tower has given her a sequence, the spacing behind the Cherokee is the controller's job alone
A 360 is the normal spacing tool in a tower pattern; controllers expect it from trainers, so there is no need to call before she makes one
questions.why: Controllers can anticipate shallow S-turns but not a 360, which can open a gap and set off a chain reaction with following traffic. A pilot who maneuvers to keep spacing should always advise the controller if at all possible, and except when requested or in an emergency, a 360 should never be made in the pattern without first advising the controller [[33:244|AIM 4-3-5]] [[33:245|AIM 4-3-5]]. The better habit is to fit the traffic before joining downwind by adjusting course or speed, then set power to avoid flying too fast or too slow [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]. Overtaking is backward in option two: the aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way, and the overtaking pilot alters course to the right [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(f)]].

questions.q: Ten miles from a nontowered airport your learner has heard nothing at all on the CTAF. She says, "Nobody's here, so let's save time with a straight-in." What do you teach?
options: Silence on the CTAF means her receiver has failed, so she should squawk 7600 at once and land at the nearest towered airport using light signals
Check volume, frequency and the mike, then fly a normal entry and scan; radios are generally not required there, so quiet is not empty
Silence on the CTAF shows the pattern is empty, so a straight-in is a sound choice as long as she announces it once before she starts down
Call UNICOM and use whatever runway the operator gives, because UNICOM must answer pilots and has to give accurate wind and runway information
questions.why: The AIM says to be alert to the lack of sounds in the receiver: check the volume, recheck the frequency and make sure the mike is not stuck [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]]; with no response, recheck the radios or use another transmitter and keep the next call short [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3]]. Squawking 7600 after a quiet stretch skips those checks. Nontowered airports generally do not require two-way radios, so pilots must be especially vigilant [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.2]], and aircraft without radios may be in the pattern [[24:170|AFH 8-6]]. If no traffic is seen, check the ground indicators to choose the runway and pattern direction [[17:4|AC 90-66C 8.2.1]]. UNICOM operators are not required to answer, and there are no standards for what they say [[17:5|AC 90-66C 9.3]].

questions.q: You brief a learner for her first visit to a nontowered airport at 2,345 feet MSL. The Chart Supplement lists a pattern altitude of 800 feet AGL, no large or turbine aircraft use the field, and she will arrive from the upwind side using the preferred entry. Which altimeter readings does she plan?
options: Cross midfield at 3,145 feet MSL, which is pattern altitude, then stay at 3,145 feet MSL around the pattern, since that is the quicker entry
Cross midfield at 3,645 feet MSL, then fly the pattern at 3,345 feet MSL, since 1,000 feet AGL is the standard for propeller airplanes
Cross midfield at 2,845 feet MSL, below the pattern, then climb to 3,345 feet MSL on the 45 so she joins downwind at 1,000 feet AGL
Cross midfield at 3,645 feet MSL or higher, descend once well clear, and fly the pattern at 3,145 feet MSL, the published 800 feet AGL
questions.why: The AIM recommends 1,000 feet AGL for propeller airplanes unless another pattern altitude is published in the Chart Supplement [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3]], and the PHAK notes that propeller pattern altitudes run from 600 to as high as 1,500 feet AGL, so always look it up [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]]. Here: 2,345 + 800 = 3,145 feet MSL, not the default 3,345. The preferred upwind-side entry crosses midfield at least 500 feet above pattern altitude [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]: 3,145 + 500 = 3,645 feet MSL. Crossing at pattern altitude is the alternate midfield entry, and crossing under the pattern is not an AFH entry at all [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. The same Chart Supplement entry gives her the CTAF [[33:207|AIM 4-1-9]], so brief both together.

questions.q: Approaching a Class D airport in clear weather, your learner's transmitter quits but she can still hear the tower. She says, "Class D requires two-way radio, so landing there is illegal now." What is accurate?
options: She may land with VFR weather, visual contact with the tower and a landing clearance; squawk 7600, wait outside until she knows the flow, then join
She is right: 91.129 bars a landing in Class D without two-way radio in all cases, so her only legal choice is to fly to a nontowered airport outside the airspace
She may land with no clearance at all, because any radio failure is automatically an emergency, and an emergency cancels every Class D requirement
She may enter straight in and land on the runway the ATIS gives, because she can still hear the tower and so meets the two-way radio rule in part
questions.why: 14 CFR 91.129(d) lets a VFR pilot whose radio fails in flight operate and land if the weather is at or above basic VFR minimums, visual contact with the tower is kept, and a clearance to land is received [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)]]. With a dead transmitter the AIM says stay outside or above the surface area until the flow is known, join the pattern, monitor the tower frequency, look for light signals, and rock the wings by day to acknowledge [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]]; squawk 7600 [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]]. Whether a radio failure is an emergency is the pilot's call, not automatic [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1]]. A quieter nontowered field can still be the prudent choice [[1:358|PHAK 14-24]], but not because landing is illegal.

questions.q: At a towered airport a business jet makes a touch-and-go on runway 27 in a light quartering wind. Seconds later the tower clears your learner, holding short in the trainer, for takeoff on 27, and she starts to roll onto the runway. What do you teach?
options: Go now: once the tower clears her, the wake behind the jet becomes the controller's problem, and refusing a takeoff clearance is not allowed
Wait at least 2 minutes after the touch-and-go, since the wake can lie along the runway; she may refuse the clearance and say unable, with why
Go now, but rotate before the jet's touchdown point and climb above its path, as when departing behind a larger airplane
Wait only until the jet's tail is past the departure end, because its vortices climb away from the runway right after it lifts off again
questions.why: After a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go, vortices settle and move sideways near the ground, so the hazard may lie along the runway and in her flight path, particularly in a light quartering wind. The AIM says to make sure at least 2 minutes have passed before the takeoff or landing [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]. Vortices sink, they do not climb [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]. The rotate-early technique is for departing behind a larger aircraft, not the touch-and-go case [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Accepting or refusing a clearance is the pilot's responsibility [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]], and "unable" means she can't comply [[34:436|AIM P/C Glossary]]; she adds the reason.

questions.q: You are teaching closed-traffic touch-and-goes at a towered airport with Runway Status Lights. Cleared for takeoff, your learner has just started rolling at low speed when the takeoff hold lights ahead turn red. She says, "Tower cleared us, keep going." What do you teach?
options: Keep going: a takeoff clearance from the tower always overrides the lights, because Runway Status Lights only confirm what the controller has already said
Stop, and then start the roll again as soon as the lights go out, because dark takeoff hold lights mean the runway ahead is now clear of traffic
Keep going and report the lights after liftoff, because takeoff hold lights warn only about vehicles crossing, never about other aircraft
Stop while she safely can and tell the tower she stopped for the lights; when they go out she still waits for a clearance before rolling again
questions.why: Red takeoff hold lights tell an aircraft in position or rolling that the runway is occupied or about to be by another aircraft or a vehicle; the pilot should safely stop if feasible or remain stopped and contact ATC [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6]]. Only when stopping is impractical does she continue on best judgment, knowing it is unsafe [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6]]. She must tell the tower she stopped for an RWSL indication, never cross red lights, and never move when the lights go out without an ATC clearance, because RWSL verifies a clearance and never substitutes for one [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6]]. THLs going out is not a takeoff clearance [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6]].

questions.q: Runway 27, wind 270 at 18 knots, left traffic. Your learner flies every pattern turn at the same 20 degrees of bank. Her turns from downwind to base leave her drifting away from the runway, and each base ends on a long final. Teaching it as the rectangular course, what do you tell her for that turn?
options: Roll in fairly steep for the high tailwind groundspeed, shallow out as it turns to crosswind, and turn more than 90 degrees
Roll in shallow and then steepen, since groundspeed is lowest on downwind and keeps rising as the airplane turns from downwind onto base
Keep the bank at 20 degrees in every turn, since a constant bank angle gives a constant radius over the ground whatever the wind
Turn exactly 90 degrees onto base and fix the outward drift later by steepening the base-to-final turn as needed to line up
questions.why: The rectangular course prepares the pilot for the traffic pattern [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. In the turn from downwind to base the AFH has the pilot roll in with a relatively steep bank, reduce it gradually as the tailwind becomes a crosswind, and turn more than 90 degrees, angling toward the inside to correct for drift [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]; on base, the airplane is crabbed into the wind so the track stays perpendicular to the extended centerline [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. The rule is higher groundspeed, steeper bank, so a constant bank cannot hold a constant track in wind [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]. Saving the fix for the base-to-final turn invites the overshoot and skidding turn; at that height be reluctant to exceed 30 degrees of bank [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

questions.q: On downwind at a towered airport, number three to land, the trainer's engine starts running rough and oil pressure is falling. Your learner says, "Declaring is overkill; we're already in the pattern. I'll just ask for an early base." What do you teach?
options: She is right: declaring is meant for fire or structural damage, so a polite request for an early base keeps the frequency calm and gets the same result
Tell the tower "minimum fuel" instead, because that phrase gets traffic priority without the paperwork that an emergency declaration brings
Declare: ATC gives her priority, an aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic, and she follows the tower's instructions
Squawk 7700 and switch to 121.5 to declare, since the emergency frequency is the one that is guarded and ATC can help her best there
questions.why: The AIH says instructors should teach that declaring an emergency when one occurs is an appropriate reaction; ATC then gives priority handling, and the learner who hesitates or decides not to decide has made a wrong decision [[25:24|AIH 1-20]]. An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other air traffic [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(c)]]. Mechanical failure is a distress condition [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Already talking to the tower, she keeps her code unless told otherwise and does not change frequency unless absolutely necessary [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]], so a switch to 121.5 is wrong. Minimum fuel is not an emergency and does not imply traffic priority [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]].

questions.q: A new learner tells you midair collisions happen mostly in haze near busy airline airports, and that with an instructor aboard the lookout is covered. Which reply fits the AFH and AIH, and what habit do you build from it?
options: He is right about haze and busy airports, so on clear days at quiet fields you let him relax the scan and focus on flying the airplane
Most midairs happen head-on at cruise altitude far from airports, so the pattern is the safest part of the flight to look inside the cockpit
Most midairs happen at night when lights are hard to judge, so scanning matters most after dark, and in daylight the instructor's lookout covers it
Most midairs happen in daylight and good visibility near uncontrolled fields below 1,000 feet, 37 percent with a CFI aboard; he owns the scan
questions.why: The AFH lists the facts: midairs generally occur in daylight, most under good visibility, most between aircraft going the same direction, and nearly all at or near uncontrolled airports below 1,000 feet [[24:170|AFH 8-6]]. One study found a flight instructor aboard in 37 percent of midairs, and if learners believe the instructor carries the lookout, they never build the habit [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. The NTSB names failure to see and avoid as the most probable cause [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]. The AFH habits join the radio and the pattern: monitor the CTAF, report 10 miles out, report entering downwind, base and final, descend to pattern altitude before entering, scan constantly and use exterior lights [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].

questions.q: At night, 15 miles from your towered home airport, the low-voltage light comes on and the ammeter shows a discharge. The trainer has one alternator and electric flaps. Your learner wants to leave every light and radio on and fly a normal full-flap landing. What do you teach?
options: Shed the nonessential loads, call ATC now, plan a no-flap landing, and if the radio dies, join the pattern and watch the tower for light signals
Leave everything on and land with full flaps as usual, since the battery will power any load for at least an hour
Turn the master switch off now with no call to ATC to save the battery, then turn it back on just before landing so the flaps and radios work
Leave everything on so the tower can see her, but stay silent on the radio until short final so that the battery lasts for the landing
questions.why: Most electrical failures are in the alternator, and the battery may give very little time: the heavier the load, the faster it drains, and a 40-amp load might empty it in 10 or 15 minutes, so shed nonessential loads at once and plan to land at the nearest suitable airport [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. Notify ATC immediately, request vectors, and with electric flaps expect a no-flap landing [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. Turning the master off kills the radios for a distress call and makes ATC lose the transponder return [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]. If the radio then fails, she stays outside or above the surface area until she knows the flow, joins the pattern, watches for lights and acknowledges at night by blinking the landing or navigation lights [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]].

questions.q: Before a dual flight to a towered airport, your learner copies ATIS Information Kilo: runway 9-27 is closed. On arrival she sees no yellow X on runway 27 and decides the ATIS is out of date, so she plans to request 27. What do you teach?
options: A closed runway always shows a yellow X or a lighted X at each end, so a runway with no X on it must have been reopened and she may request it
She should trust the wind sock rather than the ATIS, since the wind decides the runway in use at every airport, towered or not
Some closures show no X at all, so she trusts the ATIS and NOTAMs, reports Information Kilo on first contact, and briefs the runway that is in use
She should land on 27 if it looks clear, since a runway closure applies only to large aircraft when no X is shown on the surface
questions.why: A yellow X at each end often marks a temporarily closed runway, but depending on the reason, the duration and the tower's hours, a visual indication may not be present, so pilots must always check NOTAMs and ATIS for closures [[1:349|PHAK 14-15]]. ATIS carries the runways in use and construction, and stating the code on first contact lets the tower confirm she has current information [[1:339|PHAK 14-5]]. A towered airport assigns the runway [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6]], so the sock does not overrule it. A late runway change is also where habit causes slips, like the AIH pilot who turned for her usual runway [[25:84|AIH 3-33]], so have her say the new runway aloud.

questions.q: Flying with a dead radio at a Class D airport on a clear day, your learner is on short final when the tower aims a steady red light at her. She starts to flare. What do you teach her to do?
options: Land and stop on the runway right away, since steady red means stop, then wait there for a flashing green clearing her to taxi off
Go around and give way, rock the wings, make a shallow turn to the upwind side once safe, keep circling, and land only on a steady green
Continue and land with extra care, since a steady red in flight is only a general caution and a landing clearance can come later
Leave the area and divert, since steady red in flight means the airport is unsafe and she must not land there at all
questions.why: In flight, steady red means give way to other aircraft and continue circling; steady green is the landing clearance [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. "Stop" is the ground meaning of steady red, and "airport unsafe, do not land" is flashing red [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. With a dead transmitter she acknowledges in daylight by rocking the wings [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]]. Once at a safe altitude on the go-around, the AFH has her make a shallow-bank turn to the upwind side for a better view of departing aircraft [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. Alternating red and green is the extreme caution signal, not steady red [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13]].

questions.q: The ATIS gives wind 270 at 15 gusting 27 for runway 27. Your learner's POH normal approach speed is 65 knots and allows a gust adjustment. Using the common rule of thumb, what does she fly on final, and when must she go around?
options: 77 knots: 65 plus the full 12-knot gust factor, and a go-around only if she is still unstable when she passes 100 feet AGL on final
71 knots: 65 plus half the 12-knot gust factor, within the POH, and an immediate go-around if unstable below 300 feet AGL
78.5 knots: 65 plus half of the 27-knot gust, and no set go-around height, since gusty days always need big corrections close in
65 knots: gusts call for no added speed, because a faster approach makes her float, and she corrects any instability in the flare
questions.why: The gust factor is 27 - 15 = 12 knots. Many pilots add one-half of it to the normal approach speed: 65 + 6 = 71 knots, and the speed and flaps must still conform to the AFM/POH [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Adding the full factor, or half of the gust value itself, is not the rule. For a typical GA piston airplane in a traffic pattern, the AFH says to start an immediate go-around if the approach becomes unstable below 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Turbulent air calls for a power-on approach slightly above normal speed, not a slower one [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Have her read the gust from the ATIS and work the number before she calls the tower.
